newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended sharply lower with the spot November contract taking the brunt of the losses. November was down by a hefty 7.12 percent or $121 on the day to end at $1,460 a tonne. Traders said perceptions of growing prompt supplies led long holders to liquidate some of their positions ahead of Friday's expiry. Benchmark January stood $16 lower at $1,406 on scale-up trade and origin selling. The closely-watched November/January spread shrank significantly to $38 at one stage before closing at $54, down from $148 the previous day. Arabica futures in New York ended mixed in dull and range-bound dealings as speculative buying was offset by trade selling, traders said.

With turnover estimated at only 4,325 lots, traders said interest in the market was dwindling ahead of the long holiday weekend. The CSCE will be closed Thursday and Friday for the Thanksgiving holiday. Benchmark March coffee settled 0.50 cents/lb firmer, at 108.10, after ranging between 108.75 and 107.50. Spot December futures finished 0.60 cent lower at 117.15, while the remaining months closed up 0.50 to 1.15. Technically, traders said March resistance was seen near 110.20 cents, while support was pegged at 106.40 cents. Our estimate released yesterday was seen neutral to slightly bullish and had little impact on prices.

NICARAGUA - The chief of Nicaragua's coffee growers association recently said that more than 80 percent of the 1996/97 coffee harvest was at risk because of bad roads, which have been made worse by recent torrential rains. David Robleto, president of the Nicaraguan Union of Coffee Growers (Unicafe), said of the 932,165 60-kg bags that Nicaragua expects to produce in 1996/97, some 757,257 bags could be affected by the poor state of the roads. Recent torrential rains and the failure to repair roads destroyed by Hurricane Cesar in July have left almost 1,000 km of roads in coffee growing regions damaged. Nicaragua plans to export 792,000 bags of coffee in 1996/97 worth an estimated $112.65 million down from the 888,370 bags it exported in 1995/96.

SOUTH KOREA - Coffee imports in July 1996 amounted to 76,812 bags, hardly changed from last year's 76,700 bags. This brought cumulative imports in the first seven months of 1996 (January/July) up to 571,423 bags, down 14.7 percent on last year's 679,784 bags. Total imports in 1995 amounted to 1.084 million bags against 1.171 million bags in 1994. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were Indonesia (111,100 vs 54,800 bags), Colombia (79,200 vs 80,500 bags), Honduras (75,600 vs 59,200 bags) and Vietnam (73,300 vs 145,900 bags). Coffee exports in July 1996 reached 4,701 bags, which brought cumulative exports in January/July 1996 up to 40,047 bags, up from last year's 22,648 bags. Total exports in 1995 reached 49,482 bags against 38,928 bags in 1994. South Korea exports most of its coffee in the form of solubles with Russia (19,700 vs 6,500 bags) being the main market.
